subject: snail
pitch: A garden snail on an adventure. A glossy spiral shell striped in caramel, chocolate and cream, a soft grey-green body with a pebbly texture and a slimy shine, two long eye stalks with little black eyes and two short feelers below. A tiny ladybird hitches a ride on top of the shell.
reasoning:
I'm planning out realistic snail proportions and scale, then sketching the skeleton structure starting with a root foot joint and a spine chain running from tail to head.

Now I'm working out the body sweep curve, keeping the foot resting flat on the ground while the head and neck rise upward, and layering mottled grey-green coloring with a lighter underbelly for countershading. Writing the radius function...

Still building the spine chain...

Mirroring s=1 as left side using +X. Now I'm placing the shell on the back of the body, building it as a spiral sweep with growing tube radius coiled around a tilted lateral axis for that classic snail-shell look.

I'm working through the spiral geometry math to keep the shell whorls from overlapping too much—calculating how the coil radius shrinks per turn and sizing the tube radius so consecutive whorls stay roughly tangent rather than intersecting.

Working out the whorl geometry...

Working out the spiral's center and starting direction, thinking through how the whorl should wind about the X-axis so the shell opening lands at the body's front-lower side where it would naturally meet the body.

I'm checking the vertical measurements to make sure the shell, body, and stalks all align properly in height — bottom of the whorl sinking slightly into the body, shell top plus the ladybird accent landing around 0.075 total.

For the shell pattern, I'm setting up spiral stripes that follow the whorl direction using the dorsal angle coordinate, dividing it into bands and assigning caramel, chocolate, and cream colors to create a continuous striped coloring around the coil.

I'll tint the apex cream using a paint condition on the dome, and attach the shell to a mid-spine joint of the bone chain for rigidity. Then I'll place a ladybird on top by raycasting onto the shell surface, building it from a flattened red dome body, black head with white marks, spots, tiny legs, and antennae.

Modeling the ladybird body as a small scaled dome with a dark centerline, then scattering black spots across the shell using a helper that projects positions onto the ellipsoid surface, and adding a small black sphere for the head.

I'm also planning the eyes with white glint dots attached to a joint on a short stalk chain, plus simple rod legs and antennae, and considering a translucent pale-green slime trail strip extruded behind the body along the floor.

Adjusting the outline smoothing and checking placement relative to the tail, then planning the root bone and body bounding volume. For the body material, I'm layering pebbly scale textures with a countershade effect—darker greens on top transitioning to a lighter belly tone.

Applying the same scale paint to the head sphere, scaled slightly for shape, and considering whether to add a darker mid-line stripe. I'm also scattering small flattened spheres across the back as tubercle bumps, using a seeded random generator with minimum distance and a filter so they only appear on the upper surface, avoiding the shell area.

Now I'm setting up the head and jaw joints, attaching the head to the end of the spine chain and aiming it forward, then adding a small darker box part for the lower lip near the jaw, giving it a "jaw" role for the skeleton.

Working out the head sphere position and the eyestalk placements relative to it, calculating base, mid, and tip points for each stalk so they angle up and slightly outward from the shell front, then starting on the feeler positions in the same way.

Now I'm defining naming conventions for the joints and chains, using side letters for left/right stalks and feelers, and beginning to lay out the actual snail model code — setting up the root joint, body spine via a catmull curve, and chaining components with proper parent relationships.

I'm working through the body sweep radius function, shaping the shell/body profile so the tail tapers to a point while the mid and head sections widen smoothly, checking that the resulting cross-section stays above the floor at each point along the spine.

Now I'm designing the spiral shell geometry, defining how the shell's radius shrinks geometrically from base to tip and setting the tube thickness to taper proportionally along that curve.

I'm limiting cream coloring to the lip area near the tip, then thinking through how dorsal stripes should follow the tube's own rotating frame so they stay continuous along the coiled shell rather than flipping with the loop's orientation. I'll skip highlight sheen for now and move on to attaching the ladybird as a joint on the spine.

I'm setting up a helper to position ladybird parts relative to its top point, then building out the legs as small rods angled under the dome's curved edge on both sides.

I'm defining the body dome as a scaled ellipsoid sitting into the shell, scattering spots and bumps across its surface, and adding tiny glinting eyes near the front tip.
